name: Fish-scale shimmer lipstick

lead: Fish-scale shimmer lipstick uses guanine, a crystalline compound found in fish scales, to give lip colour a pearly shine. The thin crystal layers reflect light, so lips look glossy and fuller-catching rather than flat.
Shimmer lipsticks became popular from the late 1950s, and pearl shades returned strongly in the late 1990s and 2000s.

paras: The pigment is mixed into lipstick or gloss as a shimmer ingredient and worn like any lip colour. Today many shimmer products use mica, silica or bismuth oxychloride in place of fish-derived pearl.
Guanine is described as an eye irritant in hazard descriptions. It is fish-derived, which matters to people avoiding animal ingredients.

angle.text: The pigment adds a light-reflecting pearly finish to lip colour. Wearers use it for a luminous, glossy look.

lead: Fish-scale shimmer lipstick is lip colour containing pearlescent guanine, the crystalline material that gives fish scales their silvery sheen. Its payoff is a glossy, iridescent finish that catches light on the lips.[1][2]

A pearl essence extracted from the scales of the common bleak was in use in Paris in 1656, and chemist Charles-Louis Barreswil identified it as guanine in 1861. The shimmer comes from thin, transparent guanine crystal layers with a high refractive index that partly reflect and partly transmit light.[1]

Descriptions of lipstick history note that early shimmer lipsticks used a pearlescent substance from fish scales, that the brand Gala brought out a pale shimmery lipstick at the end of the 1950s, and that pearl shades were very popular in the late 1990s and 2000s. Modern shimmer products may use mica, silica or synthetic particles such as bismuth oxychloride.[2]

paras: Crystalline guanine is used in cosmetics such as shampoos, eye shadow and nail polish for a pearly effect.[1] In lipsticks, fish-derived pearl was the early shimmer ingredient before mineral and synthetic alternatives became common.[2]
Pearl essence from fish scales was in use in seventeenth-century Paris, and the guanine identification followed in 1861.[1] Shimmer lipstick reached the mass market in the late 1950s.[2]
Guanine is listed as an irritant that may irritate the eyes.[1]

timeline.event: Pearl essence from common bleak scales in use in Paris.[1]
Barreswil identifies the pearl essence as guanine.[1]
Gala introduces pale shimmery lipstick (end of the 1950s).[2]
